 Startups to watch: Solex takes hands-free sunscreen from golf to sports retail
 By Valentina Giannella 2026-11-19T16:21:00+00:00 
--> 
 Solex, a British startup selling sunscreen in a bottle with a built-in foam applicator, has appointed outdoor distributors for the UK, Ireland and France and plans a refillable version for spring 2027.
 It’s a little after noon on the 12th tee, and the sunscreen in the golf bag hasn’t moved since the first hole. The player can feel the back of the neck starting to burn. Reaching for the bottle would mean slippery palms on the grip for the rest of the round, so the cap stays shut and the sun wins.
 That small, familiar choice is the whole business case for Solex , a British startup that has put a foam applicator on top of a sunscreen bottle so athletes can reapply without ever touching the cream.
 The problem nobody was solving
 Sun protection has an awareness campaign behind it and a shelf full of formulas in front of it. What it lacks, Solex argues, is a way to make the second and third application as easy as the first.
 The company tested that idea before building anything. In a survey of just over 200 consumers, more than 60 percent said they disliked the greasy feel of standard sunscreen and around four in 10 admitted they simply forgot to reapply, according to the company. A quarter said greasy hands hurt their grip during sport.
 Source: Solex 
 Solex takes hands-free sunscreen from golf to sports retail
 Founder Peter Townsend took one lesson from the numbers: people understood the risk but found the routine a nuisance. “We are not trying to replace conventional sunscreen,” he told SGIE . “We want to own the reapplication moment.”
 A bottle that does the spreading
 The answer is a prefilled 75ml bottle, with SPF30 or SPF50 cream inside, that sells for £25 (€29) in the UK. In place of a nozzle sits a saddle-shaped pad of antibacterial foam. The user presses it against an arm, a leg or the face and spreads the cream directly, with clean hands at the end.
 Every detail assumes the user is in the middle of something. A mirror inside the cap helps with coverage around the face, a valve lets the bottle reshape as it empties and a cord hooks it onto a golf bag or backpack. According to the company, one bottle covers exposed skin around 12 to 15 times.
 Golf was the natural proving ground. Players spend four hours or more on the course in open sun, often with little shade, and a sticky hand on the grip costs shots. As summers get hotter, those long exposed rounds turn golf into something close to an extreme-conditions sport. Golf courses are also where cooling textile startup LifeLabs chose to test its CoolLife fabric instead of mountain peaks.
 Solex launched on Kickstarter on Nov. 1, 2023, reached golf retail the following year and has since shipped over 20,000 bottles to golf retailers across Europe, Townsend says. 
 The early users are enthusiastic. In a follow-up poll of golfers who had already received a bottle, 66 of 120 invitees replied: 93.9 percent rated Solex above conventional sunscreen and 48.5 percent said they reapplied more often. The company acknowledges the survey was voluntary and limited to existing users, so it measures loyalty among fans rather than demand in the wider market.
 The brand has also found its way onto bigger stages. According to the company, Team GB athletes used Solex at the Olympic Games in Paris in 2024, as did Team Europe players at the Ryder Cup , without paid endorsement deals.Golf clubs have turned into a second channel. Solex prints venue and tournament logos on the lid from 96 units upward, with delivery two to three weeks after artwork approval, so the bottle doubles as pro shop merchandise.
 The scale is still small. At full retail price, 20,000 bottles amount to about £500,000 of product ( SGIE estimate). At £25 for 75ml, or roughly £33 per 100ml, Solex also asks shoppers to pay a premium in a seasonal category built on large family bottles.
 Starting again at 65
 The man behind the bottle is not a typical startup founder. Townsend launched Solex at 65, after three and a half decades spent creating products and running companies in several countries, at an age when most of his peers were planning their retirement.
 He describes it as the project he was always heading toward. “I have always enjoyed identifying everyday problems and developing practical solutions, and Solex is perhaps the most exciting product I have worked on,” he says.
 That outlook shapes how he sees his corner of the industry. “Innovation in sport isn’t always about better shoes, clothing or equipment,” Townsend says. “Sometimes it’s about solving an everyday problem that has been overlooked for decades.”
 The health motive runs alongside the commercial one. Solex works with The Melanoma Fund , a UK charity that promotes sun safety among outdoor sports participants, according to the brand’s membership profile with the Running Industry Alliance .
 The road ahead
 The next chapter moves Solex off the fairway. Burton McCall , a UK distributor supplying high street and outdoor chains, now handles outdoor and hiking accounts in the UK and Ireland, while Nic-Impex covers specialist outdoor stores in France. Townsend says talks with further partners include pharmacies, supermarkets and general sporting goods chains.
 He believes the product sells itself once people see it used. “It is a product that can be demonstrated immediately, has a clear consumer benefit and is relevant across numerous retail sectors,” he says.
 The bigger change is a refillable system targeted for spring 2027. Customers will buy a reusable applicator once and top it up with sunscreen pouches, which the company says will cut plastic use by over 80 percent, lower the entry price and give retailers repeat sales. In the golfer survey, 86.4 percent said they were likely or certain to buy refills.
 Townsend sees the refill as the step that could turn Solex “from an innovative sunscreen accessory into an international sun protection platform.” UK patent GB2620566 covers the applicator, a European application is pending and Solex says it has filed in the US, Canada, China, Australia, Japan and South Korea.
 What’s next: finishing the refill system, signing more distributors abroad and, Townsend hints, new projects in professional sport. “The response from professional athletes, consumers and international distributors has reinforced my belief that there is a substantial opportunity to change the way people protect themselves from the sun,” he says.
 About Solex 
 Solex Sun Protection Ltd is a UK sun care company founded by Peter Townsend. It sells a 75ml sunscreen bottle with a built-in foam applicator in SPF30 and SPF50, through golf retail in several European markets and, via Burton McCall and Nic-Impex, through outdoor retail in the UK, Ireland and France. A refillable system is planned for spring 2027.
